entries.exactPassage: Where is the single point of failure? If that one part broke, would the whole chain stop?
entries.concern: The activity identifies a single point of failure as a bottleneck. A capacity/flow restriction and a component whose loss stops the system can coincide, but are not identical. A backup should address the actual dependency, including shared upstream failures.
entries.proposedWording: Identify where flow is restricted and any single point of failure. Explain whether a failure would slow the chain or stop it, and what alternative or buffer addresses that risk.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: building a system requires upfront effort. You must set up the automation. You must open the account. You must make the decision once, firmly, so you never have to make it again. Most people never do this because the upfront effort feels harder than the daily struggle. But the daily struggle never ends. The upfront effort does. The choice is between a hard once and a hard forever. The strategist chooses the hard once.
entries.category: Missing contextual explanation and specific access concern
entries.concern: The claim that one must open an account and decide once can imply compulsory account setup and no continuing review. Automation needs affordability, monitoring and adjustment, as later material partly recognises. The authored non-money later alternative is useful and should remain.
entries.proposedWording: Building an appropriate system takes initial effort and continuing review. Where financial automation is suitable and affordable, check its conditions and monitor it. A reminder, scheduled chore or default can also illustrate the principle without opening an account.

entries.concern: The feedback-loop definition describes only a self-reinforcing cycle. Feedback can also balance or counteract change, such as a spending review prompting restraint.
entries.proposedWording: Feedback loop: an effect feeds back into the system and influences what happens next. It can reinforce change or counteract it. Keep the existing leverage/implementation vocabulary and controls.

entries.concern: The savings rule says20% with no exceptions. As a universal prescription it can conflict with essential needs, irregular income or unavoidable commitments; cash-only and tracking also depend on context.
entries.proposedWording: Present these as examples to evaluate. Choose an affordable saving rule that protects essentials and can be reviewed when circumstances change. A tracking or cash approach should fit access, safety and the actual problem.
